results.alertTitle: AWS console sign-in by backdoor-svc from an external address

summary.tpReason: CloudTrail directly records successful, non-MFA console logins to the newly created backdoor-svc account from 198.51.100.42 and 203.0.113.77. The account was created minutes earlier by mirage, given an active access key, AdministratorAccess, and a login profile from 198.51.100.42; the same source then performed destructive and persistence-oriented AWS actions.
summary.fpReason: The console-login rule alone could alert on authorized external use, but the account name, creation sequence, administrator grant, no-MFA sessions, source-IP continuity, and immediate reconnaissance are incompatible with a credible normal service-account workflow.
summary.whatHappened: At 16:49Z on 2026-08-19, IAM user mirage successfully logged into AWS from 198.51.100.42 without MFA and performed rapid IAM/network/KMS reconnaissance. From that IP, mirage created backdoor-svc (16:53:35Z), created active key AKIAI99ATTACKKEY (16:54:07Z), attached AdministratorAccess (16:55:20Z), and created its console login profile (17:16:50Z). backdoor-svc then successfully logged in without MFA from 198.51.100.42 at 17:19:20Z and 203.0.113.77 at 17:24:05Z, followed by DescribeInstances from 203.0.113.77 at 17:26:25Z. Prior to the alert, mirage exposed an AWS security group to 0.0.0.0/0, launched five p3.16xlarge instances, accessed finance/HR/API-key S3 objects, stopped then deleted CloudTrail, altered EC2 user data to download and execute a shell script, and disassociated an instance profile. The same source/IP and mirage identity later created privileged GCP persistence and GPU instances.
keyEvidence: AWSCloudTrail: successful no-MFA ConsoleLogin events for backdoor-svc at 17:19:20Z from 198.51.100.42 and 17:24:05Z from 203.0.113.77; DescribeInstances followed at 17:26:25Z from the latter.

AWSCloudTrail: mirage created backdoor-svc, active access key AKIAI99ATTACKKEY, attached AdministratorAccess, and created a password login profile, all successfully from 198.51.100.42 between 16:53Z and 17:17Z.

AWSCloudTrail: mirage successfully opened all-protocol ingress to 0.0.0.0/0, launched five p3.16xlarge EC2 instances, retrieved finance/HR/API-key S3 objects, and stopped/deleted management-events-trail.

AWSCloudTrail: ModifyInstanceAttribute set user data on i-0a1b2c3d4e5f00001 to base64 content decoding to a curl download from 185.220.101.55 piped to bash; an instance profile was also disassociated.

GCPAuditLogs: mirage@pkwork.onmicrosoft.com from 198.51.100.42 created backdoor-svc-gcp and its key, granted it Owner, opened all ingress, created two a2-highgpu-8g crypto-miner instances, and retrieved confidential data.
MailGuard365_Threats_CL: phish with report.exe was allowed to mirage@pkwork.onmicrosoft.com at 15:47:27Z; sender IP was 198.51.100.42, linking the AWS source to the preceding delivery.
researchDone: Reviewed the complete AWSCloudTrail timeline from 16:30Z-19:00Z, including identity, IP, MFA status, request/response fields, and errors.

Searched all AWSCloudTrail records for backdoor-svc and both alerted IPs; only three backdoor-svc events exist, all successful/no-MFA, and no events appear after 17:26:25Z. CloudTrail deletion at 17:10Z limits confidence in subsequent AWS visibility.
Reviewed same-day Sentinel alerts; preceding alerts independently flag mirage AWS persistence, AWS resource abuse, and its initial external console login.
Reviewed GCPAuditLogs for mirage to test cross-cloud correlation; found the same 198.51.100.42 conducting persistence, data access, logging impairment, network exposure, and GPU resource creation.

Reviewed firewall telemetry for the alerted IPs and relevant payload/C2 addresses; win11a (10.0.1.50) connected to 198.51.100.42 and later 203.0.113.77, with separate PAN spyware/C2 telemetry to 192.0.2.100 and a 182,986,352-byte outbound session.
Queried Entra sign-in telemetry for mirage during 15:30Z-17:00Z; no matching records were returned. Reviewed MailGuard telemetry and found the allowed high-confidence phish to mirage.
